analysis.one_liner: Ends tax breaks that let multinational corporations shift profits offshore and pay less US tax.
analysis.headline: A bill closing offshore tax loopholes for multinationals died in committee without a hearing, despite 140 House Democrats signing on and no Republican support.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would rewrite the tax rules for US multinational companies. It would tax profits booked in foreign countries in the year they are earned instead of letting companies defer or shelter them, force companies to calculate foreign tax credits country by country so profits in low-tax havens can't be shielded by taxes paid elsewhere, limit the interest deductions multinational groups use to cut their bills, and treat companies that reincorporate abroad or are run from the US as American companies for tax purposes.
analysis.who_benefits: Federal taxpayers generally, because the bill would raise revenue by ending tax breaks that mainly benefit large multinational corporations and their shareholders. The bill's framing also points to workers, since the tax rules it targets reward companies for booking profits and operations abroad.

how_it_helps.text: It would tax the foreign profits of US multinationals in the current year and apply the rules separately to each country, so income parked in low-tax havens could no longer be blended with taxes paid in higher-tax countries to lower the bill.

It repeals the reduced tax rate on foreign income and the deduction for foreign-derived intangible income, two 2017-law provisions that let multinationals pay far less than the standard corporate rate on foreign earnings.
It limits the interest deductions that multinational groups can claim, closing a lever companies use to shift profits out of the US.

It tightens the rules for corporate inversions, so a US company that merges into a foreign shell to reincorporate in a low-tax country would generally still be taxed as domestic, and foreign corporations managed and controlled from the US would be treated as domestic for tax purposes.

analysis.who_pays: US multinational corporations and their shareholders, through higher tax bills on foreign earnings, fewer deductions, and new country-by-country reporting. Opponents would add that some of the cost could reach consumers and workers if companies adjust prices or investment.

drawbacks.text: Most provisions apply retroactively to taxable years beginning after December 31, 2022, so companies would owe more tax on past years under rules they did not have on the books when those years began.

The country-by-country accounting and reporting requirements would add real compliance costs and complexity for companies with operations in many countries, costs that fall hardest on large global businesses but eventually get priced into products.

The bill raises taxes only on US-headquartered multinationals, which critics argue could disadvantage them against foreign competitors not subject to the same rules; the bill never got a hearing, so this trade-off was never tested in markup.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets loopholes that are widely criticized for letting large multinationals pay low effective rates on offshore profits, and it would restore revenue to the Treasury. The honest costs are real but ordinary: retroactive effective dates, more compliance paperwork, and a competitiveness argument that US-headquartered firms would pay more than foreign rivals. The design is coherent, but because the committee never took it up, none of it was ever refined or debated.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Ways and Means Committee on the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up, so it sat until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Representative Lloyd Doggett introduced the bill on February 9, 2023, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Ways and Means.
140 House Democrats signed on as cosponsors; the record shows no Republican cosponsors.
No further action appears in the record: the committee never held a markup or voted, and the bill never reached the House floor before the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: US multinational corporations kept the offshore tax advantages the bill would have ended, since the committee controlled by the majority party never allowed the bill a hearing or vote.

for.name: Rep. Lloyd Doggett
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the House.

for.name: 140 of 216 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, roughly two thirds of the House Democratic caucus.

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Rep. Jason Smith (R-MO)
against.what_they_did: Took no action after referral: no markup, no vote, and no report on the bill during the two-year Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 140 cosponsors were House Democrats and no Republican signed on; with Republicans controlling the Ways and Means Committee and the House, the bill never advanced.

industries.note: The bill would end the reduced rates, deductions, and deferral rules that let multinationals pay low tax on profits booked offshore, raising their tax bills substantially. Its gains would run to the Treasury and taxpayers, not to the companies.

industries.industry: Low-tax jurisdictions and international corporate structuring services
industries.note: Tighter inversion rules and a tax on foreign corporations managed from the US would shrink the incentive to reincorporate in or route profits through tax havens, reducing demand for offshore structuring.
